value.overview: The Buff-throated Saltator (Saltator maximus) is a large, sturdy songbird of the tanager family. It has a grayish-brown back, olive wings, a pale buff throat, and a bold white eyebrow and moustache contrasting with a dark face. Its loud, ringing songs are a familiar sound in many tropical habitats. In Costa Rica, it is a widespread resident of forest edges, gardens, plantations, and other areas with dense vegetation and fruiting plants.
value.classification: The Buff-throated Saltator belongs to the family Thraupidae, the tanagers and their relatives, and the genus Saltator. It is one of several closely related saltators found in tropical and subtropical regions of the Americas.
value.identification: This saltator is about 20–22 cm long, with a heavy, conical bill and a relatively long tail. Adults are mainly olive-brown above and grayish below, with a conspicuous pale eyebrow, dark eye line, whitish moustachial stripe, and buff-colored throat. The lower breast and belly are gray to pale olive. Its repeated, emphatic song helps identify it, especially where dense vegetation makes visual observation difficult. Sexes are similar in appearance.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from Mexico through Central America and into northern and western South America. In Costa Rica, it is a widespread resident and occurs on both the Caribbean and Pacific slopes, including the northern lowlands and foothill regions. It commonly inhabits forest borders, second-growth woodland, shrubby clearings, hedgerows, coffee and cacao plantations, gardens, and parks. It generally favors habitats with thick cover and abundant fruiting vegetation, from low elevations into the foothills and lower montane zone.
value.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, the Buff-throated Saltator is generally a year-round resident rather than a long-distance migrant. Local movements may occur in response to food availability, breeding, or seasonal conditions.
value.breeding: Breeding can occur during the wetter parts of the year, with timing varying by region. The nest is a bulky open cup made from grasses, rootlets, plant fibers, and other vegetation, usually placed in a shrub, small tree, or dense tangle. The female typically lays a small clutch of pale eggs marked with darker spots. Both adults are involved in caring for the young, and the species may attempt more than one brood when conditions are favorable.
value.dietFeeding: The Buff-throated Saltator eats a varied diet of fruits, berries, seeds, buds, flowers, and other plant material. It also takes insects and other small invertebrates, particularly when feeding nestlings. It usually forages in shrubs, vines, and the lower or middle levels of vegetation, often moving methodically through cover. In gardens and cultivated landscapes, it may visit fruiting plants and consume fallen or exposed seeds.
value.behavior: This species is usually seen singly, in pairs, or in small family groups. It can be conspicuous when singing from a partly exposed perch, but it often remains within dense foliage while feeding. Pairs may defend territories with loud calls and songs. The Buff-throated Saltator is alert and quick to retreat into cover, although it adapts well to disturbed habitats and may live close to homes, farms, and other human-modified areas.

conservation.populationTrend: The species remains widespread and has a large global population, although available assessments indicate an overall decreasing population trend.
